name: Pangare (mealy)
summary: Mealy: the pale muzzle, eye rings, belly, flanks and inner legs of an Exmoor pony or a Fjord. It takes red pigment off the soft parts of the horse, which is why it shows brightest on a chestnut, spares a bay's black points entirely, and is invisible on a black. Held here as a dosage of two made-up alleles: no gene, locus, variant or DNA test for mealy has been published, and how it is inherited is unknown. The one lead is a region about 50 kb downstream of EDN3 on chromosome 22 (Jaderkvist Fegraeus et al. 2018): in 1,915 horses of 18 breeds one marker there was mostly C in pony and draft breeds, near fixed in Exmoors and Fjords where mealy is common, and mostly T in racing and show-jumping breeds where it is rare. That study was about harness-racing performance, not a study of mealy horses, so the link is indirect. Mealy is not the same thing as seal brown, though the two can look alike. It has no known effect on build, speed or the long hair.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: No mealy lightening - the underside is the same colour as the rest of the horse.

phenotypes.name: Trace pangare
phenotypes.description: A pale lower muzzle and faint rings round the eyes, and very little else. Easy to mistake for ordinary shade variation, which is why a pale muzzle on its own does not identify the trait.

phenotypes.name: Mild pangare
phenotypes.description: A pale muzzle and clear eye rings, a light underline, and soft pale patches behind the elbows.

phenotypes.name: Pangare
phenotypes.description: The familiar mealy horse: pale muzzle and jaw, an obviously light belly, groin and flank, and visible lightening up the inside of the legs.

phenotypes.name: Strong pangare
phenotypes.description: Broad cream soft areas - the pale lower face reaching up the cheeks, a creamy underside climbing the barrel, and the insides of the legs pale most of the way up. The outer legs and any black points stay dark.
